source: Smith & Vela (2001) Environmental context-dependent memory: A review and meta-analysis
finding: Changing the incidental room between study and test gives a small but reliable memory loss.
numbers: 93 effect sizes pooled: d = .28 (95% CI +/-.05). Heterogeneity large (QT = 242.47, p < .001). 83 physical-reinstatement studies: d = .28.
limits: Small average. Many studies show zero. Mostly student word lists.
agent_relevance: Expect a modest average match benefit with big swings by condition. Do not build the scaffold on the idea that matching is always strong.

source: Smith & Vela (2001) Environmental context-dependent memory: A review and meta-analysis
finding: The size of the effect depends on the paradigm. Interference-reduction designs show the biggest effect, plain reinstatement the smallest.
numbers: Reinstatement d = .23 (n = 66); interference reduction d = .68 (n = 10); multiple contexts d = .45 (n = 7); QB = 18.60, p < .001.
limits: Few studies in the two larger-effect groups.
agent_relevance: Context helps most when it separates a target from rival memories. Tag memories by what distinguishes them, not only by what matches.

source: Smith & Vela (2001) Environmental context-dependent memory: A review and meta-analysis
finding: Associative (inter-item) processing at study wipes out the room effect.
numbers: Associative processing d = .13 (n = 29); non-associative d = .33 (n = 12); unsure d = .38 (n = 42); contrast chi2 = 6.67, p < .01. Fernandez & Glenberg's null result came from 7 of 8 studies using associative processing.
limits: Coding of encoding task was by the reviewers; the 'unsure' group is large.
agent_relevance: When items are encoded with strong links to each other or to content cues, outside context stops mattering. Rich semantic encoding makes the index less context-bound.

source: Smith & Vela (2001) Environmental context-dependent memory: A review and meta-analysis
finding: Test type (free recall, recognition, cued recall) did not change the effect, against the outshining prediction.
numbers: Free recall d = .29 (n = 52); recognition d = .27 (n = 28); cued recall d = .25 (n = 3); QB = .21, n.s. Authors note lab word-list studies (Godden & Baddeley) show recall-only effects, while face and incidental-event studies show recognition effects.
limits: Cued recall had only 3 studies; the null could hide a moderator (material type).
agent_relevance: Do not assume that giving the agent a strong content cue removes the context effect in every task type.

source: Smith & Vela (2001) Environmental context-dependent memory: A review and meta-analysis
finding: Mental reinstatement of the study context helps when the physical context has changed.
numbers: Smith (1979) d = .27; Smith (1984) d = .88. Largest effect in the whole set: Krafka & Penrod d = 1.71 (but mixed mental and physical cues). Same experimenter present at test lowered the effect (d = .26 vs .62 with a new experimenter).
limits: Few clean tests; the biggest effect is confounded.
agent_relevance: Cheap move for an agent: before retrieval, restate the situation in which the memory was made. Promising, not proven.

source: Smith & Vela (2001) Environmental context-dependent memory: A review and meta-analysis
finding: Time spent in the study context did not predict the effect, which fails to support the overshadowing account in this form.
numbers: Study exposure time was not a significant predictor.
limits: Authors say this does not reject overshadowing, which is shown elsewhere.
agent_relevance: Longer exposure to a context does not by itself make it a usable cue.

source: Godden & Baddeley (1975) Context-dependent memory in two natural environments: on land and underwater
finding: Divers learned word lists on land or underwater and recalled 4 min later in the same or other place. Same-place recall was better. Not opened this session; described from the replication paper.
numbers: All four combinations per diver, completed over 4 days (per the replication paper). Original size described there as large.
limits: Free recall of word lists only. A 1980 follow-up found no effect with recognition (per Smith & Vela). Details here are secondary.
agent_relevance: Origin of the 'match the retrieval place' lesson. Underwater is not a typical agent setting.

source: Murre (2021) The Godden and Baddeley (1975) experiment on context-dependent memory on land and underwater: a replication
finding: Failed replication of the diving study. No same-context advantage and no trend in that direction.
numbers: N = 16 divers, all 4 conditions. Learning environment F(1,60) = 16.2, p < .001 (land learning better). Recall environment F = 0.601, p = .440. Interaction F = 1.999, p = .163. Learned underwater: recall on land better than underwater (p < .01).
limits: Differences from the original: all four conditions in about 1.5 h not 4 days (possible interference); lower scores; older, less educated divers; filmed for TV; underwater speakers. Underpowered for d near .25.
agent_relevance: The best-known context demonstration did not replicate in a small attempt. Weak evidence either way. Plan for small, fragile effects.

source: Murre (2021), effect-size context
finding: The replication author cites the typical free-recall room effect as d about .25, so the original diving effect was probably unusually large.
numbers: d about .25 expected; N = 16 gives low power.
limits: Interpretation by the replication author, citing the meta-analysis.
agent_relevance: Prior for any scaffold test: expect small gains, so use large samples when testing it.

source: Saufley, Otaka & Bavaresco (1985) Context effects: Classroom tests and context independence
finding: Real students tested in a different room from the lecture room did not do worse.
numbers: 253 students in the first test, 250 in the second; 21 comparisons across 7 courses, none reliable. Separate natural experiment: same context 58.5 (n = 125) vs changed 59.1 (n = 97), t < 1.
limits: Course material is learned across many places and heavily rehearsed. Rooms were not altered in a planned way.
agent_relevance: Well-learned, decontextualized knowledge does not need a matching setting. The risk is for items learned in one narrow context.

source: Fernandez & Glenberg (1985) Changing environmental context does not reliably affect memory
finding: Eight experiments with room changes failed to show a reliable context effect. Known from the Smith & Vela review, which says 7 of 8 used associative processing at input.
numbers: 8 experiments, mostly null (via Smith & Vela).
limits: Read only through the meta-analysis.
agent_relevance: Counter-evidence that created the field's doubt. Check any context claim against this null record.

source: Smith & Manzano (2010) Video context-dependent recall, Experiment 1
finding: Video scenes behind target words gave very strong context reinstatement. The effect shrank as more words shared one context (cue overload).
numbers: Cohen's d: 1 word per scene 3.02; 3 words 2.18; 15 words 1.00. Main effect F(1,318) = 648.19, eta2 = .67. Reinstated words recalled about 2x (15 per scene), 5x (3), more than 6x (1).
limits: Cues were explicit video scenes shown at test, much stronger than an ambient room.
agent_relevance: A context cue works best when it points to few items. One cue key per few memories, not one key for many.

source: Smith & Manzano (2010) Video context-dependent recall, Experiment 2
finding: Local context reinstatement replicated, with a no-scenes control to check for output-order bias.
numbers: Counterbalancing by reinstatement interaction F(1,75) = 7.21; in the no-reinstatement group words from the two conditions did not differ.
limits: Within-paper replication, same lab and method.
agent_relevance: The cue effect was selective for the cued items and not only a reorder effect.

source: Thomson & Tulving (1970) Associative encoding and retrieval: weak and strong cues
finding: Weak cues help only if present at study. Strong cues helped even if absent at study. The weak-cue result matches Tulving & Osler (1968).
numbers: Exp 1 mean words recalled: weak cue at study and test 15.7 vs 10.7 with no test cue; strong cue both 20.2 vs 12.2; no study cue plus strong test cue 19.0 vs 14.1 for none; no study cue plus weak test cue 11.1 vs 14.1 (cue made it worse); strong study cue plus weak test cue 9.2 vs 12.2.
limits: Student word lists. Sample sizes not extracted. The strong-cue reading was later challenged by Higham (2002).
agent_relevance: Core finding for the subfield. A cue that was not part of the stored encoding can hurt even versus no cue.

source: Higham (2002) Strong cues are not necessarily weak: Thomson and Tulving (1970) and the encoding specificity principle revisited
finding: Replicated the weak-cue-only pattern in free report, then showed it vanishes with forced report. Strong cues seemed to fail because of poor monitoring and a cautious report criterion.
numbers: Free-report retrieval: weak cue .24 (trial) and .29 (phase) vs no cue .08; strong cue not above no cue (F < 1). Forced report: strong .25/.27, weak .26/.31, no cue .08; strong and weak both beat none (p < .001). Mean confidence: weak cues 3.41, strong cues 1.84.
limits: Word-pair material with a pay-off schedule; about 48 participants (F(1,45)). Report option is a lab construct.
agent_relevance: Poor cues lead to withheld answers, not necessarily lost memories. Force a guess or a ranked read-out when cues are poor.

source: Santa & Lamwers (1974), reported in Higham (2002)
finding: Telling people that test cues are strong associates of the targets removed the failure of strong cues.
numbers: No warning, strong cue: 5.33 words, equal to no cue (5.40). Warned: 10.07 words.
limits: Described secondhand in Higham 2002.
agent_relevance: Instruction about how a cue relates to the target changes how it is used. Tell the agent how the cue was made.

source: Goh & Lu (2012) Testing the myth of the encoding-retrieval match, Experiments 1 and 2
finding: Rival account (Nairne 2002): cue diagnostic value, not raw match, drives recall. Higher match helped only when the cue pointed to few other targets.
numbers: Exp 1 (N = 40): low overload, high match .37 vs low match .24, F(1,39) = 17.14; high overload .28 vs .28, F < 1; interaction F(1,39) = 13.89. Exp 2 (N = 42): .31 vs .20 at low overload; .24 vs .23 at high overload; interaction F(1,41) = 5.23.
limits: Word pairs in the lab; undergraduates in Singapore.
agent_relevance: Match only helps if the cue picks out one item. Build distinctive keys; do not add matched words to an overloaded key.

source: Goh & Lu (2012), Experiment 3
finding: Replicated Thomson & Tulving: the originally studied cue, even weak, beat a strong new cue. Cue overload cut recall sharply.
numbers: N = 40. Low overload .31 vs high overload .14, F(1,39) = 90.24. Cue type: intralist weak cue .32 > strong extralist cue .25 > weak extralist cue .09 (p < .05 and p < .001); no interaction.
limits: Same lab; undergraduates.
agent_relevance: Keep the original encoding cue stored with the item. It is a strong resource.

source: Shin, Masis-Obando, Keshavarzian, Dave & Norman (2021) Context-dependent memory effects in two immersive VR environments: On Mars and underwater
finding: With two very different VR worlds (Mars, underwater) plus a schema task, same-context recall was higher. The effect was larger for items judged relevant to the world.
numbers: 72 adults recruited, 64 analysed (32 same, 32 different). Same .32 vs different .26; beta = 0.349, SE = .130, Wald Z = 2.69, p < .01. Overall accuracy .29. Delay condition showed the benefit (16 per group); immediate condition did not; the interval interaction was not significant.
limits: Authors combined many factors to get an effect, so they cannot say which are needed.
agent_relevance: A context effect appears when the context is meaningful to the task. Relevance to the item matters more than visual match.

source: Shin et al. (2021), schema moderator
finding: Items judged useful for the environment gained more from matching context than items judged harmful.
numbers: Congruency by usefulness interaction significant; 52% of items judged useful; no difference in keep rate between environments (beta = .098, p = .362).
limits: Judgments came from participants, so the split is not randomized.
agent_relevance: Context cues link best to items processed in relation to the context. Encode the why, not only the where.

source: Eich and colleagues, state-dependent memory (1980 to 1995), as framed by Smith & Vela
finding: Outshining boundary: context effects are strong in free recall and can vanish when a good explicit cue is supplied. Not opened this session.
numbers: No numbers collected.
limits: Known only through the Smith & Vela framing; not checked against the originals.
agent_relevance: Prefer an explicit content cue over hoping that a context match will retrieve; fall back to context when no good cue exists.

source: Nairne (2002) The myth of the encoding-retrieval match
finding: Argues the encoding-retrieval match alone cannot predict recall; cue diagnostic value (how few traces the cue fits) matters. Known through Goh & Lu (2012), which tests it.
numbers: See Goh & Lu entries.
limits: Not opened directly.
agent_relevance: Design retrieval keys to be distinctive. Test rather than assume.

source: Tulving & Wiseman (1975) Relation between recognition and recognition failure of recallable words
finding: Proposed a function relating recognition to recognition failure of recallable items. Later challenged (a 1998 paper argues for rejecting it on item-specific effects). Not opened.
numbers: No numbers collected.
limits: Only titles seen in a search listing.
agent_relevance: An item can be recalled but not recognised: retrieval depends on the exact cue, not stored strength alone.

source: Dinh, Ding, Qu & Thilakarathna (2026) Memory Retrieval in Transformers: Insights from the Encoding Specificity Principle
finding: Maps queries to retrieval context, keys to trace index, values to content. Swapping keys and values changes what the model recalls.
numbers: Swap V: counterfactual answers in 50% (OLMo-2) to 90% (Qwen2.5). Swap K+V: 100% hallucination on factual prompts in all models. Swap K only: factual accuracy about 30% to 40%, no hallucination. Models: Llama 2 7B/13B, Llama 3.1 8B, Qwen 2.5 14B, Phi-4, GPT-NeoX-20B, OLMo-2.
limits: Preprint; the mapping to psychology is the authors' interpretation.
agent_relevance: Supports the view that keywords in the prompt act as cues for what the model recalls. Put the exact terms the memory was written with into the retrieval prompt.

source: Dinh et al. (2026), keyword perturbation
finding: Blocking attention to identified keywords cut recall of memorised text far more than blocking random words.
numbers: In OLMo 2 13B, perturbing all heads at keywords sharply reduced ROUGE-L recall and BERTScore; random-word perturbation had minimal effect. Text: Project Gutenberg books.
limits: Memorised book text, not new episodic content. Llama 2 showed little difference across keyword methods.
agent_relevance: Model recall hinges on a few salient tokens. Mismatch in those tokens can break recall.

source: Nogueira, Yang, Lin & Cho (2019) Document Expansion by Query Prediction (doc2query)
finding: Adding predicted user questions to each document at index time improves search. This is writing the cues at encoding.
numbers: BM25 + doc2query improved effectiveness by about 15% on MS MARCO and TREC-CAR. Recall@1000 on MS MARCO dev 85.3 to 89.3. Query expansion with RM3 hurt on both sets.
limits: Fine-tuned seq2seq model, not an LLM agent. Gain is relative to BM25 only.
agent_relevance: Engineering analogue of 'encode the cue you will need at retrieval'. Store likely retrieval queries with each memory.

source: Gao, Ma, Lin & Callan (2022) Precise Zero-Shot Dense Retrieval without Relevance Labels (HyDE)
finding: Writing a hypothetical answer first and searching with it improves retrieval. It moves the cue toward the encoded form.
numbers: TREC DL19 nDCG@10: Contriever 44.5, BM25 50.6, HyDE 61.3. DL20: Contriever 42.1, BM25 48.0, HyDE 57.9. Recall@1k DL19: HyDE 88.0 vs Contriever 74.6.
limits: InstructGPT text can be wrong; the dense encoder filters it. Gains vary by dataset.
agent_relevance: At retrieval, rewrite the cue into the form of the stored note, and test against the plain query.

source: Gutierrez, Shu, Gu, Yasunaga & Su (2024) HippoRAG
finding: Indexing entities as a graph and spreading activation from cue entities gave better multi-hop retrieval.
numbers: Recall@5 average over MuSiQue, 2Wiki, HotpotQA: HippoRAG (ColBERTv2) 72.9 vs ColBERTv2 65.6 vs BM25 58.4. 2Wiki R@5 89.1 vs 68.2. HotpotQA R@5 77.7 vs 79.3, where ColBERTv2 is better.
limits: Gain is mostly on multi-hop sets.
agent_relevance: Linking cues to related items lets a partial cue reach the target.

source: Temporal Context Reinstatement Drives Episodic-Like Order Memory in Long-Context Language Models (2026)
finding: Long-context models show the human distance effect in order memory; performance seems to rely on a time code reinstated by a single attention head. Only the abstract was seen.
numbers: No numbers collected.
limits: Abstract only.
agent_relevance: A model-internal analogue of context reinstatement. Not yet a result to lean on.

source: Human-Inspired Memory Architecture for LLM Agents (2026)
finding: Agent memory system with hybrid multi-cue retrieval; on LongMemEval it matched raw retrieval at a 200K-token budget. Only the abstract was seen.
numbers: 70.1% vs 71.2% accuracy, overlapping 95% CI; preference recall +13.3 pp at S-tier scale with dedup-based consolidation.
limits: Abstract only; the multi-cue part is not isolated from five other mechanisms.
agent_relevance: Multi-cue retrieval is in use; no clean ablation of it was seen.
